lessons.0.slides.0.description: A quantitative understanding of climate change's real impact
lessons.0.slides.1.title: 🌍 1970–2026: Fifty Years of Climate Change History
lessons.0.slides.1.content: **1970s: Stable Traditional Climate** — Annual mean temp 11.5 °C; typical harvest 25 Sep–5 Oct; extreme heat days 2–3/yr; frosts occasional and predictable; style: high acid, elegant, mineral. **1980s: First Warming Signals** — Rose to 11.8 °C (+0.3 °C); 1983 first truly hot year; harvest 5–7 days earlier; scientists began tracking global warming. **1990s: Warming Trend Established** — 12.3 °C (+0.8 °C vs 1970s); hot years 1990, 1997, 1999; harvest moved to mid-September; alcohol rose from 12.5 % to 13 %. **2000s: Extreme Events Begin** — 12.8 °C (+1.3 °C); 2003 historic heatwave (45 °C peak); 2006 severe frost; drought frequency rising; insurance costs climbing. **2010s: The New Normal** — 13.0 °C (+1.5 °C); 2012 hail, 2013 mildew, 2016 spring frost; three consecutive scorching years 2018–2020; harvest moved to early September; 13.5 % alcohol the norm. **2020s: Crisis and Adaptation** — 13.3 °C (+1.8 °C); 2021 catastrophic spring frost (50–80 % crop loss); 2022 extreme drought; 2023 major mildew outbreak; harvest advanced to late August; domaines began major technical adjustments. **Key milestones** — 1988: IPCC founded; 2003: European heatwave shocked the wine world; 2015: Paris Climate Agreement; 2020: France permitted emergency irrigation for classified vineyards; 2026: Burgundy designated a climate-change research priority zone.
lessons.0.slides.2.title: Alarming Rate of Warming
lessons.0.slides.2.content: Over the past 50 years (1970–2020) Burgundy's average temperature rose approximately 1.8 °C, well above the global average of 1.1 °C. Summer days above 35 °C increased from 2–3 per year to 10–15. Spring frost risk grew as earlier budburst meets later frosts. Rainfall patterns shifted: wetter winters, drier summers. These changes have reshaped Burgundy's terroir, affecting ripening, flavour, alcohol, and acid balance.
lessons.0.slides.3.title: 📊 Key Climate Data (1970 vs 2020)
lessons.0.slides.3.points.5: Frost risk: medium → high (due to earlier budburst)
lessons.0.slides.4.title: 🌡️ Burgundy Annual Mean Temperature 1970–2026
lessons.0.slides.4.content: Temperature has risen 1.8 °C over 56 years, faster than the global average. Every decade sets a new record; the 2020s have already reached 13.3 °C.
lessons.0.slides.5.title: 📅 Harvest Date Advancement: Gevrey-Chambertin Case Study
lessons.0.slides.5.content: Harvest has advanced by 35 days over 40 years — close to one day per year. What once began in early October now starts in late August, reshaping the entire winemaking rhythm and decision pressure.
lessons.0.slides.6.title: Alcohol and Acid Balance Over Time
lessons.0.slides.7.title: 💡 Increase in Extreme Heat Days (>35 °C)
lessons.0.slides.7.content: Extreme heat days surged from 2–3 per year to 10–15 over 50 years, greatly raising the risk of grape sunburn. The 45 °C peak in 2003 shocked the entire industry.
lessons.0.slides.8.title: 1990s vs 2020s Comparison
lessons.0.slides.9.title: Increase in Extreme Weather Events
lessons.0.slides.9.content: The 2003 European heatwave, the 2016 major frost, three consecutive hot years 2018–2020, and the catastrophic 2021 spring frost (50–80 % crop loss) illustrate accelerating extreme-event frequency. Traditional climate models have broken down; growers need new strategies to cope with uncertainty. Insurance costs have skyrocketed, straining smaller producers.

lessons.1.slides.1.title: 📅 Harvest Date Evolution: Gevrey-Chambertin Case Study
lessons.1.slides.1.content: **1980s — Traditional Rhythm** — 1985: 1 Oct (sugar 220 g/L, acid 7.2 g/L); 1988: 28 Sep (221 g/L, 7.0); 1989: 18 Sep (first early-ripening year, 235 g/L, 6.5). **1990s — Warm New Normal** — 1990: 22 Sep (230 g/L, 6.8); 1996: 24 Sep (classic year, 218 g/L, 7.5); 1999: 15 Sep (240 g/L, 6.2). **2000s — Accelerating Advance** — 2003: 27 Aug (earliest ever, 258 g/L, 5.0); 2005: 20 Sep (perfect balance, 228 g/L, 7.0); 2009: 12 Sep (245 g/L, 5.8). **2010s — Frequent Extremes** — 2015: 7 Sep (242 g/L, 6.0); 2018: 29 Aug (252 g/L, 5.2); 2019: 5 Sep (248 g/L, 5.5). **2020s — Records Keep Falling** — 2020: 24 Aug (255 g/L, 5.0); 2022: 20 Aug (second earliest ever, 260 g/L, 4.8); 2023: 8 Sep (mildew reduced yield but high ripeness). **Key observations** — Harvest advanced 35 days over 40 years (≈1 day/year); sugars: 220 → 250 g/L (+13 %); acidity: 7.0 → 5.0 g/L (–28 %); alcohol: 12.5 → 14.5 % (+2°); harvest window: 2–3 weeks → 1 week; decision-making pressure: error margins greatly narrowed.
lessons.1.slides.2.title: Harvest Advanced by 30 Days
lessons.1.slides.2.content: In the 1980s Burgundy's average harvest ran 25 Sep–5 Oct; by the 2020s it had moved to 25 Aug–10 Sep — a full 30-day advance. This reshapes the entire winemaking rhythm: the cellar must be prepared earlier, labour is harder to schedule (university students are still in class), and holidays conflict. More critically, the traditional strategy of 'waiting for peak ripeness' no longer applies; growers must make rapid decisions balancing sugar, acid, and tannin.
lessons.1.slides.3.title: 📅 Harvest Date Evolution (Gevrey example)
lessons.1.slides.4.title: Physiological Ripeness vs Phenolic Ripeness
lessons.1.slides.5.title: The Acid-Retention Dilemma
lessons.1.slides.5.content: High temperatures cause malic acid to decompose rapidly, driving acidity down. Traditional Burgundy reds had 6–7 g/L; now 5–6 g/L is common. Low-acid wines lack freshness, have weaker ageing potential, and are more prone to oxidation. Domaines face a difficult choice: harvest early to retain acid (but phenolics are unripe) or wait for phenolic maturity (but acidity is lost). Some domaines now add tartaric acid (legally permitted), though this risks undermining a 'natural' image.
lessons.1.slides.6.title: 🍇 New Considerations in Harvest Decisions
lessons.1.slides.6.points.0: Weather forecast: monitor closely 7–10 days out
lessons.1.slides.6.points.1: Taste the grapes: taste daily; don't rely solely on sugar readings
lessons.1.slides.6.points.2: Harvest in passes: different parcels ripen at very different rates
lessons.1.slides.6.points.3: Night harvesting: keep grapes cool and slow oxidation
lessons.1.slides.6.points.4: Fast decisions: shorter window; very little room for error
lessons.1.slides.6.points.5: Experience built fresh: historical data less reliable; rely on present judgement
lessons.1.slides.7.title: 💡 Managing High Alcohol
lessons.1.slides.7.points.0: Early harvest: sacrifice some ripeness to preserve acidity
lessons.1.slides.7.points.1: Selective picking: remove over-ripe bunches; retain freshness
lessons.1.slides.7.points.2: Adding water: prohibited in France (permitted in Italy and the US)
lessons.1.slides.7.points.4: Natural fermentation: indigenous yeasts may reduce alcohol by ~0.5 %
lessons.1.slides.7.points.5: Accept reality: 13.5–14 % is the new normal

lessons.2.slides.1.title: 🏆 Top Domaine Adaptation Strategies: Case Studies 2015–2026
lessons.2.slides.1.content: **DRC — Biodynamic Response**: raised soil organic matter to 8 % (water retention +35 %); increased Preparation 500 from 2 to 4 applications per year; increased canopy shade cover from 30 % to 50 %; in 2022 carried out emergency irrigation at La Tâche for the first time. Result: even in extreme drought, acidity held above 5.5 g/L. **Leroy — Extreme Low-Yield Strategy**: yields down to 12–15 hl/ha (legal limit 35); only 2–3 bunches per vine (normal: 20); 100 % whole-cluster fermentation (stems balance alcohol); night harvesting (from 3 a.m.). Result: 2020 wine at 14.8 % yet still elegant. **Leflaive — White Wine Technical Innovation**: harvest 7–10 days earlier to protect acidity; cold maceration 24–48 hours (aromatics, not phenolics); extended barrel ageing to 18 months; new oak reduced to 20 %. Result: Puligny-Montrachet retained its classic mineral style. **Jadot — Plot Restructuring**: sold overly hot south-facing plots in 2018; invested in Hautes-Côtes at 450 m; acquired 20 ha in northern Marsannay; trialled NE-facing slopes. Result: a portfolio better suited to future climate. **Rousseau — Technology-Assisted**: 30 soil-moisture sensors installed in 2020; AI system predicts optimal harvest date (85 % accuracy); drone infrared monitoring; precision irrigation (activated only at stress thresholds). Result: 2022 drought caused only 15 % loss (neighbours: 30 %). **Dujac — Winemaking Innovation**: whole-cluster fermentation up from 30 % to 80 %; fermentation temp down to 26 °C; maceration shortened from 21 to 14 days; bottling brought forward 6 months. Result: at 13.8 % alcohol, still showing Morey elegance. **Common trends**: all top domaines increased whole-cluster fermentation; water retention became top priority; night harvesting increasingly widespread; tradition and technology combined; 14 % alcohol accepted as the new norm.
lessons.2.slides.2.title: Vineyard Management Adjustments
lessons.2.slides.2.content: Domaines are adopting multiple strategies to cope with warming: 1) retaining more leaves for shade; 2) cover-cropping to conserve moisture; 3) moderate irrigation (now permitted for emergencies); 4) adjusting pruning to slow ripening; 5) trialling new heat-tolerant clones; 6) changing row orientation to reduce sun exposure. These adjustments require years of trial and test the technical skill and patience of each producer.
lessons.2.slides.3.title: 🌿 Vineyard-Level Strategies
lessons.2.slides.3.points.0: Shade management: retain more leaves; prevent fruit sunburn
lessons.2.slides.3.points.1: Cover crops: vegetative cover retains moisture and lowers soil temperature
lessons.2.slides.3.points.2: Emergency irrigation: French law relaxed in 2020; classified sites now permitted
lessons.2.slides.3.points.3: Soil management: increase organic matter; improve water-holding capacity
lessons.2.slides.3.points.4: Frost-protection equipment: fans, candles, heaters (use surged after 2021)
lessons.2.slides.3.points.5: Risk diversification: multiple plots at different altitudes and aspects
lessons.2.slides.4.title: Traditional vs Adaptive Management
lessons.2.slides.5.title: Winemaking Technique Adjustments
lessons.2.slides.5.content: The cellar also demands adaptation: whole-cluster fermentation is increasing (stems provide tannin balance); maceration is shortened (avoid over-extraction); fermentation temperatures are lower (preserve aromatics); older oak barrels are used more; bottling is earlier (reduce oxidation risk). These adjustments aim to counterbalance the higher alcohol and lower acidity that warming brings, preserving Burgundy's hallmark elegance.
lessons.2.slides.6.title: 🍷 Winemaking Innovations
lessons.2.slides.6.points.1: Cold maceration: extended cold soak to extract aromatics without tannin
lessons.2.slides.6.points.2: Gentle extraction: avoid over-extraction; preserve elegance
lessons.2.slides.6.points.3: Old oak: reduce new oak to 20–30 % (avoid overwhelming the fruit)
lessons.2.slides.6.points.4: Longer ageing: extend barrel maturation; add complexity

lessons.3.slides.1.title: 💰 Parcel Revaluation: 2010 vs 2026 Price Comparison
lessons.3.slides.1.content: **Strongly Appreciated (>100 % gain)** — Chablis Grand Cru Les Clos: €350,000/ha (2010) → €900,000/ha (2026, +157 %); perfect ripeness + retained high acidity. Marsannay Clos du Roy: €120,000 → €280,000 (+133 %); a marginal village transformed. Hautes-Côtes de Nuits: €80,000 → €200,000 (+150 %); high-altitude advantage now fully apparent. Fixin Les Hervelets: €150,000 → €320,000 (+113 %); quality leap in northern villages. **Steady Appreciation (50–80 %)** — Gevrey village (north-facing slopes): €450,000 → €720,000 (+60 %); northern aspect retains elegance. Meursault village (high-altitude): €600,000 → €950,000 (+58 %); whites relatively unaffected. **Slower Appreciation (<30 %)** — Pommard village (south-facing low slopes): €400,000 → €480,000 (+20 %); over-heating risk suppresses demand. Corton Grand Cru (south slopes): €1,200,000 → €1,400,000 (+17 %); Grand Cru status but climate challenges mounting. Volnay village (SE flat): €500,000 → €580,000 (+16 %); plain heat-island effect. **Benefiting plots**: altitude 400 m+; north-facing slopes; Chablis appellation (biggest winner); clay soils (better water retention). **Challenged plots**: low altitude (<300 m); south-facing slopes; sandy soils (drought stress); flat terrain. **Investment outlook**: Chablis +50–80 % over the next decade; Marsannay/Fixin undervalued; Hautes-Côtes no longer secondary; traditional Grands Crus still hold value but slower growth.
lessons.3.slides.2.title: The Rise of Northern and High-Altitude Sites
lessons.3.slides.2.content: Warming is reshuffling parcel values: once-too-cold plots (Hautes-Côtes, northern Chablis) now achieve ideal ripeness; once-perfect sites (Corton south slopes) risk overheating. Marsannay, Fixin, and other northern villages have seen quality surges. Chablis climate now resembles what Meursault was in the past — a region that may appreciate dramatically over the next 20 years.

lessons.3.slides.4.title: Benefiting vs Challenged Plots
lessons.3.slides.5.title: Chablis's Golden Age?
lessons.3.slides.5.content: Chablis may be the greatest beneficiary of climate change. Once plagued by underripeness and frost, a 1.5 °C rise has produced perfect ripeness while retaining high acidity and minerality. Five consecutive great vintages from 2015–2020 demonstrate the new climate's potential. William Fèvre and Raveneau are making wines that approach Puligny quality. In the future, Chablis Grand Cru could rival Montrachet.

lessons.4.slides.0.description: Looking 30 years ahead at the future of the terroir
lessons.4.slides.1.title: 🔬 2050 Scientific Prediction Model Comparison
lessons.4.slides.1.content: **IPCC Models (6th Assessment, 2023)** — SSP1-1.9 (highly optimistic): Burgundy +0.5–0.7 °C by 2050 (total +2.3 °C vs 1970); mean 13.8 °C; harvest 5–10 Sep; alcohol 13.8–14.2 %; acid 5.2–5.8 g/L; Pinot Noir: good, traditional style maintained; probability 15 %. SSP2-4.5 (moderate, current policies): +1.2–1.5 °C (total +3.0–3.3 °C); mean 14.5–14.8 °C; harvest 20–25 Aug; alcohol 14.5–15.0 %; acid 4.5–5.2 g/L; extreme events double; Pinot Noir: difficult; probability 50 % (most likely). SSP5-8.5 (pessimistic, high emissions): +2.0–2.5 °C (total +3.8–4.3 °C); mean 15.3–15.8 °C; harvest 10–15 Aug; alcohol 15–16 %; acid 4.0–4.5 g/L; extreme events ×3–4; probability 20 %. **BIVB local model** — Côte de Nuits (250–350 m): maintainable in optimistic; major challenge in moderate; only high-altitude north-facing sites in pessimistic. Chablis: winner in all scenarios; peaks in moderate. Hautes-Côtes: goes from secondary to core even in moderate. **Scientist consensus**: warming 100 % certain; magnitude depends on decarbonisation; Pinot Noir is Burgundy's greatest challenge; 2020–2030 is the critical decade; immediate sustained adaptation is essential.
lessons.4.slides.2.title: IPCC Climate Model Projections
lessons.4.slides.2.content: Under the IPCC moderate-emissions scenario (RCP 4.5), by 2050 Burgundy's average temperature will rise a further 1–1.5 °C (total +3 °C vs 1970), equivalent to today's northern Rhône Valley climate. Extreme weather will double in frequency, frost risk persists, and summer drought becomes standard. The optimistic scenario limits warming to 0.5–0.8 °C if global carbon neutrality succeeds.
lessons.4.slides.3.title: 🌡️ 2050 Scenario Projections
lessons.4.slides.4.title: Pessimistic vs Optimistic Scenarios
lessons.4.slides.5.title: The Survival Question for Pinot Noir
lessons.4.slides.5.content: Can Pinot Noir survive in Burgundy at +3 °C? Optimists argue that clonal selection, viticultural technique, and winemaking innovation can adapt. Pessimists worry: Pinot Noir is acutely sensitive to heat — is a 14.5 % Pinot still Pinot? Some domaines are already privately trialling heat-tolerant varieties (Syrah, Grenache), though these remain prohibited by AOC law. Future regulations may need revolutionary revision.

lessons.4.slides.8.title: Epilogue: What Changes and What Stays
lessons.4.slides.8.content: Over its millennium of history Burgundy has survived countless changes: phylloxera, wars, industrialisation, globalisation. Climate change is a new challenge, but Burgundy's core — its obsession with terroir, its pursuit of quality, its respect for tradition — will not change. The Burgundy of 2050 may look different, but it will remain a beacon for wine the world over. Our responsibility: to understand the change, adapt proactively, and pass on the spirit.
